proposals.name: Mechanistic explanation of a phenomenon, not only a performance delta
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the abstract's contribution is an account of WHY something happens, as opposed to a report that a new construction scores better. A 10: the abstract names a puzzling or consequential phenomenon and offers a specific causal account of its origin, such that a reader ends with a changed model of how the object behaves (e.g. vulnerability traced to linearity; trainability traced to depth scales of signal propagation; a training behaviour traced to an implicit bias of the optimizer rather than the loss). A 5: a mechanism is gestured at ('we analyze', 'sheds light on') but the abstract's substance is still a method plus its wins. A 0: the abstract contains no causal claim at all - it identifies a gap, proposes machinery, and reports that the machinery works. Do not reward mere use of the word 'theory'; reward an explanation that could be stated in one sentence and could be wrong.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high half is thick with abstracts whose payload is an explanation rather than a delta: R02 replaces nonlinearity/overfitting accounts of adversarial examples with a linearity account and derives the cross-architecture transfer fact from it; R24 explains trainability by depth scales of information propagation and predicts what dropout does to that critical point; R20 explains contrastive learning via augmentation overlap; R59 explains in-context learning as latent-concept inference. The dense-low/card-high half is largely explanation-free (R48, R50, R21). A scorecard built from checkable properties of a write-up has little purchase on 'this abstract changed my model of the object', so it under-credits exactly this.

proposals.name: Stakes a risky thesis against a prevailing belief
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract commits to a claim that a competent reader could have disagreed with before reading, and states it flatly rather than hedging. A 10: an explicit contradiction of an accepted position or of a standard practice, phrased as a claim ('we argue instead that the primary cause is X'; 'this component can be removed with little or no loss'; 'the widely adopted assumption hardly holds'), including cases where the abstract reports that a well-regarded prior method misbehaves. A 5: mild disagreement framed as an incremental limitation of prior work. A 0: no position is staked; the abstract only asserts that a gap exists and that the authors fill it, with all claims of the safe form 'our method performs better'. Score the riskiness of the proposition, not the confidence of the prose.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('We argue instead that the primary cause ... is their linear nature'), R25 (a whole layer of standard practice declared to have marginal value), R18 (the perceptual loss declared superfluous) and R10 (a celebrated method shown to behave 'arrogantly, directly at odds with convergence') all sit dense-high with card at or below .56. By contrast R43 and R53 stake nothing contestable. A fixed criterion bank can score clarity, novelty-claim and evidence, but a proposition's riskiness is a property of the field's priors rather than of the text's surface, so the scorecard misses it.

proposals.name: Subtractive contribution: shows an accepted ingredient is unnecessary
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the contribution is the REMOVAL of something the field currently assumes it needs - a loss term, a training stage, a data requirement, a layer, an integrator, a tuning burden - with evidence that quality survives the removal. A 10: the central claim is 'you do not need X', with the abstract stating what was removed and that performance is retained or improved. A 5: a simplification is claimed alongside a larger set of additions. A 0: the contribution is purely additive - new modules, new losses, new stages layered onto an existing pipeline. Removals must be of things currently believed necessary; dropping an obviously optional extra scores low.
proposals.rationale: Subtraction is concentrated on the dense-high side: R25 (do not train the last weight layer), R18 (adversarial supervision alone suffices, perceptual loss dropped), R38 (task-specific priors for detection dropped in favour of plain sequence prediction), R35 (a deliberately simple spectral filter replacing deeper machinery). All four carry card_pct <= .56 while dense_pct runs .545-.868. A criterion bank naturally rewards presence of components and evidence about them; an absence has nothing to score, so removals read as thin. R44 and R28, which are the additive extreme, sit card-high.

proposals.name: Reframing that yields what the old framing could not
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract recasts its problem into a different formalism AND shows the recasting buys something specific the original framing could not deliver - a new algorithm, a new estimator, a bound, or a removed requirement. A 10: the reframing is load-bearing (e.g. graph convolution recast as an integral transform, which licenses Monte Carlo estimation and hence batched training without test data present; detection recast as sequence prediction, which lets task priors be dropped). A 5: a reframing is announced and something modest follows. A 0: no reframing, or a purely nominal one - a unifying vocabulary under which existing methods are re-derived, with practice left unchanged. Judge the consequence, not the elegance of the vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R38 both convert a problem into another formalism and immediately cash it out (batched training plus inference generalization; minimal task assumptions), and both sit dense-high with card in the .3-.46 band. R32 is the instructive contrast: a genuine unifying algebraic perspective under which prior 1-Lipschitz layers are re-derived, but the practice it authorizes is close to what existed - and it sits dense .218 / card .821. A scorecard can verify that a unifying framework is claimed; it cannot easily verify that the frame did any work.

proposals.name: Question sits at a live shared concern, with stakes made legible
proposals.instruction: Score the combination of (a) how many researchers' work is touched by the question and (b) whether the abstract makes that reach visible without inflating it. A 10: the question is one many groups are actively blocked on, and the abstract's first lines locate it there concretely (why neural nets break under tiny perturbations; why large models learn from prompts; why graph nets cannot be trained on large graphs; why large-batch training stalls). A 5: a real but specialist question, competently situated. A 0: a narrow technical corner or a single application, with the stakes asserted rather than shown ('X is important in many pipelines') and no indication that anyone outside the subfield is waiting on the answer. Do not reward topical fashionability alone - reward that a resolution would unblock others.
proposals.rationale: Every strongly dense-low item in this slice is peripheral to the field's live concerns even when technically sound: R30 (permutation orders for 1-dimensional strongly convex functions, dense .056 / card .521), R46 (linkage-based clustering algorithm selection, dense .013 / card .632), R57 (multi-view priors from sparse viewpoint data, dense .105), R40 (wavelet covariance texture synthesis, dense .188), R01 (SDE integrator-free estimation, dense .060). The dense-high extreme is the opposite: R02, R41, R59, R09. Centrality is a property of the surrounding field, not of the text, so a text-local criterion bank cannot see it - which is precisely why these rows disagree.

proposals.name: Economy of mechanism relative to size of the consequence
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio between how little the method asks and how much it claims. A 10: a mechanism statable in one clause (prune activations at random and rescale; freeze the classifier up to a scale; use a single modified diffusion kernel) paired with a consequence that is large, qualitative, or surprising. A 5: moderate machinery, moderate payoff. A 0: an elaborate apparatus - several new losses, encodings, hypernetworks, schedules, regularizers - whose stated payoff is a benchmark improvement of ordinary size. Penalize expensive-for-what-it-buys; reward cheap-for-what-it-buys. This is about the ratio, not about simplicity or ambition alone.
proposals.rationale: R25, R36, R38 and R35 are all one-clause mechanisms carrying outsized claims and all sit dense-high with card .103-.457. The card-high side concentrates the opposite ratio: R28 spends its abstract on three named components plus a multi-task training procedure, R44 stacks a content-preservation loss, a CLS matching loss, a CLIP loss, a semantic divergence loss and a resampling strategy, R43 defines three amalgamation mechanisms plus perturbations. A bank of criteria scored independently and summed rewards each additional described component, so it systematically prices apparatus as evidence of substance.

proposals.name: Idea-to-apparatus ratio in how the abstract spends its words
proposals.instruction: Score how the abstract allocates its own text. A 10: most words go to the claim, the reason it should hold, and what follows from it; named parts appear only as needed. A 5: an even split between idea and inventory. A 0: the majority of the abstract is an inventory of the authors' own machinery - enumerated contributions ('our contributions are three-fold', 'i) ... ii) ... iii) ...'), coined component names, and acronyms introduced for parts rather than for the whole - with the reason any of it should work left implicit. Judge allocation of text, not length: a very short abstract that is all idea scores high.
proposals.rationale: R28 and R43 read as parts catalogues and sit card .761 and .893 against dense .291 and .214; R21 similarly (card .927). At the other pole R39 spends two sentences entirely on the construction and the claim (dense .996 / card .338), and R24, R25 and R58 are idea-dominant with card .030-.252. Enumerated components are exactly what an itemized bank can find and credit, so word-count spent on apparatus converts into scorecard points while the dense reader is measuring how much idea per paragraph.

proposals.name: Qualitative capability change versus incremental margin
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract reports a change of kind rather than of degree. A 10: something previously impossible or impractical becomes routine, and the abstract says so concretely - orders of magnitude in time or scale, a regime opened (training that took days now takes an hour and a quarter; verification on networks an order of magnitude larger than any complete verifier had handled; the first exact determination of a quantity). A 5: a solid but ordinary improvement on an established number, stated precisely. A 0: a small percentage gain on a standard metric presented as the paper's headline. Score the character of the change; a precisely stated small gain is still a small gain.
proposals.rationale: R41 (three days to 76 minutes), R54 (two to three orders of magnitude faster, first exact adversarial accuracy) and R09 (orders of magnitude cheaper training) are dense .979, .987 and .904 with card .568, .393 and .316. The card-high side reports careful but ordinary margins as its headline: R48 (1.6% Top-1 with 0.16M added parameters), R56 (10.9% and 12.4% MAE). A judge scoring 'are quantitative results reported' cannot distinguish a well-reported small gain from a regime change, and the well-reported small gain often looks better on such an item.

proposals.name: Guarantee binds the method actually used
proposals.instruction: Score whether formal results in the abstract constrain the object the authors are proposing, on the assumptions they operate under. A 10: a proved statement about the proposed construction, whose content is what a practitioner would worry about (convergence and saddle avoidance for the actual algorithm across the full class of games; stability and non-dissipativity of the actual architecture, with the two consequences named; an identity that licenses the actual training objective; a size bound shown to be near-optimal in the parameter that matters). A 5: theory about a simplified proxy of the method, with the gap acknowledged. A 0: no formal content, or a theorem whose hypotheses clearly do not cover the method as used, or one whose conclusion is irrelevant to any concern a user would have.
proposals.rationale: The most extreme card-low rows in the slice are precisely the papers whose payload is a binding guarantee: R10 (card .038), R22 (card .073), R60 (card .047), R42 (card .068), with dense at .342-.474 - a large gap in every case. These abstracts have no benchmark tables, no dataset lists and no code links, so an itemized bank scoring evidence-of-results finds almost nothing to award, while a reader who understands that 'proved, and it binds' is the strongest evidence available reads them as substantial.

proposals.name: Engages a specific named prior claim, including partial disconfirmation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract takes up an identified prior claim - a named conjecture, algorithm, assumption or result - and reports precisely what survives contact and what does not. A 10: the prior claim is identified specifically, and the outcome is differentiated (true in the linear case and for the reason the earlier authors did not identify, false in the nonlinear case; the widely adopted independence assumption is shown unnecessary; the celebrated method is shown to fail in a stated way). Reporting that one's own analysis only partly vindicates a hypothesis counts strongly here. A 5: prior work is named but only as a baseline to beat. A 0: prior work appears only as an undifferentiated mass ('existing approaches', 'recent methods') that the paper improves on.
proposals.rationale: R14 takes up the Dai and Wipf conjecture and returns a split verdict - true for linear encoders/decoders and due to implicit bias rather than the loss, false in general in the nonlinear case - and sits dense .321 / card .034. R10 does the same to LOLA and R20 to the conditional independence assumption (card .038 and .197). Against this, R53 and R55 engage only 'existing approaches'. Specific engagement with a named claim is invisible to a bank scoring 'is related work positioned', and a partial disconfirmation reads on such a bank as a weaker result rather than a more honest one.

proposals.name: Finding is shown to hold across settings, not only in the demonstration
proposals.instruction: Score evidence in the text that the finding is a property of the class of systems rather than of the particular setup: claims of invariance across architectures, datasets, hyperparameters, bit-widths, or regimes, offered as part of the result rather than as a closing hope. A 10: the transfer is intrinsic to the claim (a phenomenon that generalizes across architectures and training sets and is explained by that generality; depth scales that apply to any randomly initialized network; one stored weight set quantizable on demand to arbitrary bit-widths). A 5: results on several datasets within one narrow task family. A 0: a single dataset, task or application domain, with generality only asserted in the last sentence ('may have advantages beyond', 'plausibly downstream tasks').
proposals.rationale: R02 makes cross-architecture, cross-training-set transfer part of the explanandum, R24 states depth scales for random networks in general, and R29 turns bit-width invariance into the deliverable itself - dense .944, .363 and .769 against card .436, .030 and .427. The card-high side often has broader tables but narrower findings (R27, a zebrafish classifier; R57, one street-scene dataset), and hedged generality (R15's 'plausibly', R51's 'may have advantages beyond'). Counting evaluation settings, which a bank does well, is not the same as judging whether the finding itself travels.

proposals.name: Experiments probe the stated explanation, not just the headline metric
proposals.instruction: Score whether the empirical work described is designed to test the paper's own account of why the method or phenomenon behaves as it does. A 10: the abstract names a measurement, a constructed dataset, or a derived quantity whose only purpose is to check the explanation (a metric derived from the theory and shown to track the quantity the theory predicts; a small synthetic corpus built so that the predicted phenomena can be exhibited and falsified; a regularizer designed so that the mechanism it presumes can be observed). A 5: standard benchmarks reported, with one diagnostic or ablation tied to the mechanism. A 0: only aggregate performance on standard benchmarks, so that the paper's story about why it works is untested by anything reported.
proposals.rationale: R20 derives an unsupervised model-selection quantity from its augmentation-overlap account and checks that it tracks the predicted target (dense .545 / card .197); R59 builds a synthetic corpus specifically so its latent-concept explanation can be exhibited, along with the order-sensitivity and scaling predictions (dense .731 / card .389); R02 supports its linearity claim with new quantitative results and with the transfer fact it predicts. R05, whose claimed contribution is a principle about spectral invariance, reports only that extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness (dense .855 / card .188) - showing the scorecard is scoring the presence of experiments, not their evidential fit to the claim.

proposals.name: Headline rests on an idea rather than on a leaderboard position
proposals.instruction: Score what the abstract's central claim would reduce to if the numbers were removed. A 10: a statable proposition survives - something is true, something is unnecessary, something works for this reason. A 5: an idea and a ranking claim share the load. A 0: nothing survives - the claim is exhausted by breadth and rank ('a large-scale protocol comprising N baselines, M search spaces and K datasets; we achieve new state-of-the-art'), so that the paper's identity is its position on a table. Breadth of evaluation is not penalized in itself; it is penalized when it is the whole of the claim.
proposals.rationale: R50 is the pure case - a protocol of 12 baselines, 16 search spaces and 86 datasets, ending in a rank claim - and sits card .966 against dense .385; R56 (card 1.000 / dense .094), R48 (.919 / .568) and R21 (.927 / .449) are the same shape. R24, R25 and R58 lose nothing if their numbers are struck out, and sit card .030, .162 and .218. An itemized bank scores evaluation breadth, baseline count and result strength as separate positive items, so a paper whose only claim is a leaderboard position accumulates points on several items at once.

proposals.name: Recombination justified by a specific failure it uniquely fixes
proposals.instruction: Score, for abstracts whose contribution is bringing technique X to problem Y, whether the pairing is derived or merely analogized. A 10: a specific failure of the current approach to Y is identified, and X is shown to be the thing that addresses that failure - ideally with the connection made formally (quantization modeled as a bounded perturbation, from which the particular gradient penalty follows). A 5: a plausible but unforced pairing with a stated benefit. A 0: motivation of the form 'inspired by the success of X in other domains, we apply it to Y', or justification by convenience ('it is a by-product of the framework and comes at no extra cost'), with no argument that Y specifically required X. Papers that are not recombinations should be scored on whether their central move is similarly forced by the problem.
proposals.rationale: The dense-low/card-high half is dominated by convenience pairings: R21 adopts hyperbolic uncertainty as the pacing signal largely because it is a free by-product of the chosen geometry (card .927), R53 applies coordinate-based neural representations to network weights by analogy with visual signals (card .697), and R06, R16 and R51 follow the same import-a-technique shape. R29 is the contrast - the perturbation model of quantization forces the specific regularizer, dense .769 / card .427. A criterion bank can check that motivation is present; checking that the motivation forces this particular pairing requires knowing the space of alternatives.

proposals.name: Substantive, checkable content actually present in the text
proposals.instruction: Score whether the item contains enough content to be judged at all, and whether its central claim is specific enough that a reader could name the observation or argument that would refute it. A 10: the claim is concrete and its refutation is imaginable. A 5: real content, but the central claim is stated only as effectiveness or promise. A 0: there is no content to assess - a title with no body, a stub, or text consisting entirely of unfalsifiable promise. Brevity by itself is NOT a low score: a two-sentence abstract that names a construction and commits to a claim about it scores well above a long abstract that commits to nothing. Absence of text must score 0 rather than defaulting to the middle.
proposals.rationale: R04 carries no abstract text whatsoever - a title alone - and yet lands at card .902, which shows the scorecard aggregate can reach a high rank with nothing to score, presumably by defaulting rather than abstaining. R39 is the discriminating contrast: two sentences only, but it names a construction and commits to a claim about it, and reads dense .996 against card .338 - so the scorecard is penalizing shortness where the dense reader is rewarding commitment. A floor item that hard-zeros absent evidence, and that separates brevity from emptiness, fixes both halves of that error.

proposals.name: Abstract length and clause-elaboration volume
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much prose there is and how elaborated it is. 0 = a title with no abstract at all, or a single sentence; 2 = two or three sentences; 4 = roughly 60-120 words; 6 = roughly 120-200 words; 8 = roughly 200-300 words; 10 = over 300 words with many multi-clause sentences, parenthetical asides, subordinate elaboration and restatement. Count volume of text and syntactic elaboration only. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writing is clear, or whether the content is substantive; a very long text and a very short text can both be excellent or terrible and that is irrelevant here.
proposals.rationale: Sheer text volume is a classic driver of any criterion-bank aggregate, because more words give more criteria something to fire on, while a dense end-to-end reader is comparatively indifferent to it. In this slice the extremes line up with the disagreement axis: R27 has NO abstract text whatsoever (title only) and R06 is two sentences, R55 and R28 are short single-paragraph texts, and all sit in the dense_high_card_low half or otherwise carry depressed card_pct (R55 card_pct=0.145, R28 card_pct=0.162); at the other end R40 and R13 are sprawling 250-350 word texts with card_pct=0.761 and card_pct=1.000. Word count is not research quality.

proposals.name: Density of explicit numeric performance figures
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many distinct concrete numeric figures about results appear in the text: percentages, point gains, named-metric values (accuracy, FID, mIoU, MAE, RMSE), speedups, wall-clock times, parameter/FLOP counts, counts of datasets/baselines/languages compared. 0 = no numbers at all; 2 = only a symbolic or asymptotic expression, no measured quantity; 5 = one or two concrete measured figures; 8 = three or four; 10 = five or more, most of them attached to a named metric or benchmark. Score only how many such figures are stated and how concretely. You must NOT verify them, NOT judge whether the numbers are large, impressive, fair, or well chosen, and NOT reward or penalise the presence of quantification as good or bad practice.
proposals.rationale: Numerals are the easiest thing for an explicit criterion to detect and reward, so a scorecard built from written criteria will track them far more tightly than a model reading holistically. R13 (card_pct=1.000) states '10.9% and 12.4% improvement in Mean Absolute Error' and R23 (card_pct=0.910) states six separate compression/accuracy percentages; R31 (card_pct=0.919) lists 1.6% Top-1, 0.16M parameters, 0.07B FLOPs and 3-4% AP. Against them, R09 (card_pct=0.030), R12 (card_pct=0.038) and R50 (card_pct=0.047) contain no measured figure anywhere. Whether an abstract chose to print its numbers is a reporting habit, not the quality of the work behind them.

proposals.name: Enumerated contribution scaffolding and numbered-pitfall templates
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much explicit enumeration scaffolding the text uses: phrases like 'our contributions are three-fold', 'two common pitfalls: (1) ... (2) ...', 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...', 'We address this in two ways', numbered or lettered lists of problems or components. 0 = no enumeration language at all; 3 = a single ordinal marker used in passing; 6 = one clearly enumerated two-item list; 8 = an explicit contribution count plus an enumerated walkthrough; 10 = the whole abstract is organised as a numbered walkthrough of three or more items with an announced count. Score the presence and prominence of the enumeration template only. You must NOT judge whether the abstract is well organised, whether the enumerated contributions are real, or whether this structure aids the reader.
proposals.rationale: This is a learnable writing template that makes an abstract trivially parseable by criterion-by-criterion scoring: each numbered item hands the judge a discrete thing to credit. Every clear instance in the slice sits on the same side of the disagreement: R40 ('Our contributions are three-fold. First ... Next ... Finally'), R17 ('First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...'), R02 ('two common pitfalls: (1) scalability ... (2) interpretability'), R48 ('Our contribution is two-fold. First ... Second ...') and R44 ('First ... Then ... Finally') are all dense_low_card_high, with card_pct from 0.517 to 0.893. Adopting a template is a stylistic habit, not evidence about the research.

proposals.name: Proof-and-analysis genre framing versus benchmark-report framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the text's claims are stated as formal mathematical results rather than as measured benchmark outcomes. Look for: 'we prove', 'we show the existence of', theorems, bounds, convergence rates, asymptotic complexity, duality, phase transitions, characterisations of when something holds. 0 = purely an empirical report with no formal claim; 3 = mostly empirical with one formal aside; 6 = a balanced mix of a theoretical result and a benchmark table; 9 = predominantly formal results with a small illustrative experiment; 10 = entirely theoretical, with no experiments mentioned at all. This is a genre classification only. You must NOT judge whether the theory is deep, whether the experiments are adequate, or whether theoretical or empirical work is more valuable.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: which sub-community and reviewer pool an item is routed to is an unseen process factor, and its textual fingerprint is exactly the proof-versus-benchmark register. A criterion bank written in the vocabulary of empirical validation will systematically under-fire on the theory register. The six lowest card_pct items in the whole slice are all in that register: R09 (card_pct=0.030, mean-field depth scales), R59 (0.034, VAE landscape and implicit bias), R12 (0.038, convergence guarantees in differentiable games), R50 (0.047, functional ELBO and a KL supremum theorem), R33 (0.064, influence-function bounds) and R01 (0.068, coreset size bounds with near-optimality). Genre membership is not quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: subfield and reviewing-track composition the submission is routed into

proposals.name: External application-domain framing rather than core-method framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the text is anchored in an application domain outside core machine learning — astrophysics and remote sensing, biology or animal behaviour, medical or aerial imagery, chemistry and molecules, video games, street scenes, industrial deployment. Evidence: a domain motivation sentence, domain-specific datasets or instruments named, domain jargon, an audience of domain experts addressed. 0 = purely core-ML framing throughout (datasets are generic ML benchmarks); 5 = core-ML method with one domain application demonstrated; 10 = the domain problem frames the entire abstract from first sentence to last. Score only the extent of external-domain framing. You must NOT judge whether applied or core work is more valuable, nor whether the application is important.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: the unseen factor is which audience the work was written for and routed to; its visible fingerprint is domain vocabulary and domain datasets. This clusters hard on one side of the disagreement here: R35 (astrophysical multispectral imaging, card_pct=0.709), R39 (zebrafish swim-bout classification, card_pct=0.688), R57 (street-view, aerial and medical images, card_pct=0.667), R60 (street scenes, card_pct=0.645) and R47 (SMILES molecular structures, card_pct=0.513) are all dense_low_card_high. Explicit criteria reward a concrete grounded problem statement; a holistic reader weights it differently. The choice of framing audience is not research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: the sub-community the authors write for, and the reviewer pool that framing draws

proposals.name: Artifact-availability boilerplate and repository URLs
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much code/model/data release boilerplate the text carries. 0 = no mention of any artifact; 3 = a future-tense promise only ('we will release'); 5 = a bare present-tense claim with no address; 7 = an explicit repository URL; 9 = a URL plus models or pretrained checkpoints; 10 = a URL plus models plus explicit reproduction-and-extension language. Score the presence and prominence of the boilerplate only. You must NOT visit the link, NOT assess whether the artifact would actually reproduce anything, and NOT treat releasing or not releasing as good or bad practice.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: an unseen factor is whether the group had the engineering staff, legal clearance and lab convention to ship a repository; the textual fingerprint is one sentence of boilerplate that any criterion bank with an availability or reproducibility criterion will reward directly. In the slice the boilerplate concentrates on the high-card side: R13 (card_pct=1.000), R43 (0.932), R31 (0.919), R25 (0.927), R44 (0.893), R23 ('Open code for reproducing and extending our results is provided', card_pct=0.910), R02 (0.637); note also R04's weaker future-tense variant ('We will publicly release both datasets'). Tagged mixed because a well-resourced group plausibly both ships code AND does better work, so this must be reported in both bands.
proposals.upstream_parent: engineering and institutional resources of the producing group, plus its lab's release norms

proposals.name: Resource-footprint and scale-of-evaluation disclosures
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text advertises the size of the experimental apparatus, independently of its outcomes: the number of baselines, search spaces, datasets, tasks or languages covered; large-scale corpora or models trained (ImageNet, BERT, large multilingual corpora); named hardware (TPU pods, large clusters); very large batch sizes; multi-day training budgets. 0 = no apparatus scale is stated; 3 = one standard small benchmark; 5 = one or two named large benchmarks; 8 = an explicit inventory of many benchmarks or baselines; 10 = both a large inventory and named large-scale hardware or training budgets. Score how much apparatus scale is disclosed. You must NOT judge whether the evaluation is adequate, whether the resources were well spent, or whether large-scale work is better.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: compute access is an unseen, strongly unequal upstream factor; its fingerprint is the boastable inventory of scale, which explicit coverage/thoroughness criteria reward almost mechanically. R10 recites '12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks' and sits at card_pct=0.966; R58 names a TPUv3 Pod, batch size 32868 and a 3-days-to-76-minutes budget; R16 advertises 'up to 44 languages' across IWSLT/WMT/TED; R25 lists three established datasets plus downstream tasks (card_pct=0.927). Tagged mixed honestly: resources plausibly cause genuinely stronger work as well as a more impressive-sounding apparatus.
proposals.upstream_parent: compute budget and institutional resources available to the producing group

proposals.name: Density of non-native or uncopy-edited English usage slips
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how frequently surface usage slips appear that a professional copy-editor would remove: missing or extra articles, subject-verb or number disagreement, non-idiomatic verb complements, calqued phrasing, tense slips. The KIND of thing to count (these examples are about form, not merit): 'The most GCNs suffer the performance loss', 'A-DGN yields to improved performance', 'we task humans with revise each document', 'takes less epochs to find'. 0 = no slips, reads as fully copy-edited; 3 = one slip; 5 = two or three; 8 = slips in roughly half the sentences; 10 = slips in most sentences. Score frequency of surface usage slips ONLY. You must NOT judge whether the exposition is clear or the research is good, must NOT count technical jargon, heavy notation, or long sentences as slips, and must NOT infer anything about the authors.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: access to editing help (a native-speaker senior coauthor, a lab writing pass, a paid editor) is an unseen resource; the fingerprint it leaves is precisely the absence of small usage slips. Judges scoring written criteria are known to be sensitive to surface fluency even when told not to be. In this slice the visible slips cluster on the dense_high_card_low side: R29 ('The most GCNs suffer the performance loss', card_pct=0.103), R03 ('yields to improved performance', card_pct=0.073), R04 ('task humans with revise each document', card_pct=0.333) and R19 ('takes less epochs', card_pct=0.303). Tagged mixed because editing access correlates with resources that may also raise real quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author language background and access to professional editing or senior-coauthor polish

proposals.name: Named prior work cited inside the abstract, with venue or year
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much named-citation apparatus appears inside the abstract itself: prior work referred to by author surname, by year, or by venue acronym — for example '[Feldman and Schulman, SODA'12]', 'Recent work by Dai and Wipf (2020)', 'proposed by Kipf and Welling', 'Semmelhack et al. (2014)'. 0 = no prior work named (generic 'recent studies' or 'existing approaches' does not count); 4 = one named reference; 7 = two named references, or one carrying a venue and year; 10 = three or more, or several with bracketed venue acronyms and years. Score only how much such apparatus is present. You must NOT judge whether the positioning is fair or accurate, whether the cited work is the right work, or whether crediting predecessors in an abstract is good practice.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: who the authors are and which lineage they sit inside are unseen; the fingerprint is whether they can name-and-beat specific predecessors, with venue acronyms, in the abstract. Communities differ sharply in this etiquette, and a criterion bank that asks about positioning-against-prior-work will fire unevenly as a result. R01 carries three bracketed venue citations (SODA'12, FOCS'18, FOCS'22) yet card_pct=0.068; R59 names 'Dai and Wipf (2020)' at card_pct=0.034; R39 builds on 'Semmelhack et al. (2014)' at card_pct=0.688; R52 opens on 'the GCN recently proposed by Kipf and Welling'. Citation etiquette is a community habit, not research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authors' embeddedness in an established research lineage, and the citation etiquette of their home community

proposals.name: Text-preparation provenance tells: markup residue, encoding artifacts, non-US spelling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how many tells about the authoring and conversion pipeline survive in the text: unrendered LaTeX commands (\emph{...}, \url{...}, \mathbb, \mathcal, \ell), HTML entities left in place ('k>1'), Unicode math characters mixed into LaTeX math ('$ε$-coreset', '$β$-NLL'), stray quoting conventions (''on the fly''), and non-US spellings (optimise, optimised, hypothesise, behaviour, neighbourhood, modelled, regularisation, favour). 0 = clean plain prose, US spelling, no markup residue; 3 = one such tell; 6 = a few tells of one kind; 8 = several tells of more than one kind; 10 = markup or encoding residue throughout, or consistent non-US orthography together with markup residue. Count the tells only. You must NOT judge whether the formatting is sloppy or careless, must NOT treat either spelling convention as correct, and must NOT let notation-heavy content by itself raise the score.
proposals.rationale: MODE-2 reasoning: the unseen factors are which toolchain produced the submission and where the authors were trained; both leave purely mechanical traces that carry no information about the research yet vary systematically across the slice and can shift a text-only judge. R23 leaves both an HTML entity ('k>1') and raw '\emph{projective clustering}' and sits at card_pct=0.910; R01 mixes '$\mathbb{R}^d$' with a Unicode epsilon in '$ε$-coreset' at card_pct=0.068; R42 leaves a bare '\url{...}'; and the non-US orthography cluster spans R12 ('optimise'), R51 ('hypothesise'), R57 ('optimised', 'regularisation') and R29 ('neighbourhood'). None of these is research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: authoring toolchain and export pipeline, plus the regional academic training of the author group

proposals.name: Theoretical rigor without quantitative validation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 based on whether the abstract's central contribution is a formal theoretical result (a proof, guarantee, exact bound, or characterization, e.g. 'we prove', 'we show that X converges') that is reported with ZERO concrete accuracy/benchmark percentages anywhere in the text. A 10 = the abstract's entire payload is a stated theoretical result with no empirical percentage/score numbers at all. A 0 = the abstract reports concrete accuracy/benchmark numbers with no formal theoretical result stated (pure empirics, or neither theory nor numbers). Score abstracts blending both proportionally in between, weighted toward whichever mode carries the paper's main claim.
proposals.rationale: R21 (dense_pct=0.321, card_pct=0.034), R22 (0.363/0.030) and R23 (0.474/0.068) are all pure-proof abstracts with no benchmark numbers, and the scorecard crushes them to near-zero percentile while the dense model treats them only moderately-low, not crushed -- suggesting the scorecard specifically penalizes theory-without-numbers far more harshly than the dense reader does.

proposals.name: Density of precise, verifiable quantitative claims
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how many specific, checkable numbers (percentages, exact counts of datasets/baselines/tasks, precise benchmark scores) the abstract reports about its OWN results. A 10 = multiple precise numeric claims tied to the paper's findings (e.g. exact percentage gains, exact counts of baselines/datasets compared). A 0 = the abstract describes its results using only qualitative hedge words ('competitive', 'comparable', 'effective', 'significant improvement') with no numbers at all.
proposals.rationale: R47 (card_pct=0.966) enumerates '12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks' and R55 (card_pct=1.000) states '10.9% and 12.4% improvement in MAE', both scorecard-favored; by contrast R01 (card_pct=0.103) says only 'competitive' and 'comparable to other state-of-the-art methods' and R60 (card_pct=0.197) reports no numbers at all, both scorecard-punished -- numeric density tracks the scorecard's score closely.

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanation of why, not just that, it works
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central contribution is an EXPLANATION of why or how a phenomenon occurs (a causal or mechanistic account that could generalize beyond the one method shown), versus simply reporting that a new method outperforms a baseline without explaining an underlying mechanism. A 10 = the abstract's main payload is a mechanistic/causal account of a phenomenon. A 0 = the abstract only reports an engineering result (method X beats method Y) with no explanatory claim about why.
proposals.rationale: R48 (dense_pct=0.944) argues the primary cause of adversarial vulnerability is networks' linear nature -- an explanatory account -- and R37 (dense_pct=0.731) explains in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference over a latent document concept; both are dense-favored. By contrast R26 (card_pct=0.910, dense_pct=0.372) is a pure engineering compression result (SVD-style embedding factoring) with no explanatory mechanism claim, and is scorecard-favored instead.

proposals.name: Assumption-overturning or counter-intuitive claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly frames its finding as contrary to a prior belief or standard practice (e.g. 'we show X is unnecessary/superfluous', 'contrary to X we find Y', 'despite common assumption Z, we show...'). A 10 = the abstract's main claim is explicitly framed against an overturned assumption or removed requirement. A 0 = the claim is a straightforward incremental extension/improvement with no such framing.
proposals.rationale: R12 (dense_pct=0.868) shows the long-standard perceptual loss is 'superfluous' for GAN-based image synthesis, and R46 (dense_pct=0.722, titled 'Fix your classifier') shows the last weight layer need not be trained at all -- both explicitly overturn a standing assumption and are dense-favored. R16 (card_pct=0.761), which frames itself as merely 'attempting to bridge' two existing subfields via incremental architecture changes, carries no such overturning claim and is scorecard-favored instead.

proposals.name: Cross-field conceptual borrowing vs within-field survey
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract recasts its problem using a formalism or toolkit imported from a genuinely different field/subfield (e.g. treating detection as language modeling, treating graph convolution as an integral transform, treating a defense as a minimax game), enabling reuse of that other field's tools. A 10 = a clear import of an unrelated field's framework to reframe the problem. A 0 = the abstract instead surveys/unifies existing variants WITHIN its own subfield under one umbrella without importing tools from elsewhere.
proposals.rationale: R02/Pix2seq (dense_pct=0.799) casts object detection as language modeling, R28/FastGCN (dense_pct=0.904) casts graph convolutions as integral transforms solved via Monte Carlo, and R17 (dense_pct=0.991) casts adversarial defense as a minimax game from game theory -- all dense-favored cross-field imports. By contrast R04 (card_pct=0.821, dense_pct=0.218) unifies existing 1-Lipschitz layer variants under one algebraic/SDP condition WITHIN the same subfield, without importing an outside toolkit, and is scorecard-favored instead.

proposals.name: One-sentence conceptual compression vs multi-module apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how compressible the abstract's core contribution is: can it be restated in one clear sentence naming a single mechanism, or does justifying the result require enumerating three or more separately-named sub-components/modules that must act together? A 10 = a single, clean, one-sentence-summarizable core idea. A 0 = the abstract explicitly lists three or more distinct named sub-components (e.g. i/ii/iii) required for the method to work.
proposals.rationale: R40 (dense_pct=0.996) is a 3-sentence abstract built on one idea (higher-dimensional attention via tensor products). By contrast R16/PAPO (card_pct=0.761) explicitly enumerates three components -- 'population-size encoding', 'a hypernetwork', and 'population size as an additional input' -- and R30/HYSP (card_pct=0.927) layers self-supervision, hyperbolic uncertainty, and a learned pace mechanism together; both multi-component abstracts are scorecard-favored over the single-idea one.

proposals.name: Breadth across qualitatively distinct task types
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract demonstrates (or claims) the method works across qualitatively DIFFERENT kinds of tasks or architecture families (not just more datasets of the same task). A 10 = explicit evidence spanning distinct task types or architecture families (e.g. classification AND clustering AND generation; or both attention-based and convolutional architectures). A 0 = validated only on one narrow application/dataset within a single task type.
proposals.rationale: R01/S2GC (dense_pct=0.618) is tested across text, node, and graph classification, clustering, AND community prediction -- five distinct task types -- and R38/LAMB (dense_pct=0.979) works across both BERT-style attention models and ResNet convolutional models. Both are dense-favored despite (or in R01's case, alongside low card) breadth. By contrast R49 (card_pct=0.688) validates only on zebrafish swim-bout classification and R41 (card_pct=0.709) only on astrophysical/remote-sensing source separation -- single-niche applications that are scorecard-favored.

proposals.name: Named sub-problem plus explicitly generic reusable solution
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on a composite: does the abstract (a) explicitly name a previously under-addressed sub-problem as its motivating gap, AND (b) explicitly claim its solution is a generic/reusable framework applicable beyond the one instance shown (e.g. 'suitable across different architectures, datasets, and tasks')? A 10 = both a named specific sub-problem and an explicit generality claim are present. A 0 = neither is present (the paper just applies a known technique to a single setting with no generality claim).
proposals.rationale: R55 (card_pct=1.000, the highest card score in the slice) names the specific gap 'automated approaches [to label-encoding search] are lacking' and explicitly claims RLEL is 'suitable across different architectures, datasets, and tasks' -- yet its dense_pct is only 0.094, near the bottom. R47 (card_pct=0.966) similarly opens by naming HPO as 'one of the primary open questions in AI' and offers a meta-learned surrogate framework, with dense_pct only 0.385. Both extreme scorecard-favored outliers combine named-gap plus generality framing without a correspondingly high dense score, suggesting the scorecard over-credits this rhetorical combination on its own.

proposals.name: Judgability from printed text alone, no title recognition
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the item text itself (title + abstract body) contains enough substantive description of motivation, method, and results to be judged on its own, without needing to recognize the paper from its title. A 10 = the abstract body fully describes what was done and found in prose. A 0 = the abstract body is missing or is a content-free stub (title only, or a placeholder), such that any score would have to rely on recognizing the paper rather than reading its content.
proposals.rationale: R20 ('Quasi-Recurrent Neural Networks') has literally no abstract body -- only a title -- yet still receives card_pct=0.902, a very high scorecard percentile, which is only explicable if the judge scored based on recognizing this as a well-known paper rather than from the (absent) text, a direct violation of text-only scoring. Contrast with R42 (card_pct=0.145), which is also short but contains real content (a stated problem, method, and general result) and receives a much lower, more text-grounded card score -- showing the gradient this criterion should track.

proposals.name: Specificity of named failure modes in prior work
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how specifically the abstract diagnoses concrete ways existing/prior approaches fail, before presenting its own solution. A 10 = the abstract names multiple specific, concrete shortcomings of prior approaches (not a generic 'existing methods have limitations' sentence). A 0 = the abstract states no problem diagnosis at all, or only a single generic sentence about limitations, before jumping to the method.
proposals.rationale: R08 (card_pct=0.632) diagnoses that 'it is often not clear which algorithm will give the best performance' and that combining distance metrics 'often require[s] a non-trivial combination', yet has dense_pct=0.013, the single lowest dense percentile in the entire slice. R55 (card_pct=1.000) likewise diagnoses two distinct specific prior approaches' shortcomings (direct regression and generic binary-encoding). Both are scorecard-favored via detailed problem diagnosis. By contrast R40 (dense_pct=0.996) opens directly with 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer...' with zero problem-diagnosis text at all.

proposals.name: Ordinal enumerated contribution-listing rhetorical structure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly enumerates its contributions using ordinal markers ('First, ... Second, ... Third, ...', 'N-fold', 'i) ... ii) ... iii)'). A 10 = an explicit ordinal/numbered list of contributions or components appears in the text. A 0 = the abstract states its contribution as a single flowing narrative with no such enumeration.
proposals.rationale: R57 (card_pct=0.551, dense_pct=0.154) uses an explicit 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...' structure; R59 (card_pct=0.513, dense_pct=0.081) states its contribution is 'two-fold'; R16 (card_pct=0.761, dense_pct=0.291) states it is 'three-fold' with i/ii/iii components. All three enumerated-structure abstracts are scorecard-favored with notably low dense percentiles, while R40 (dense_pct=0.996) has no enumeration at all.

proposals.name: Genuinely new primitive vs recombination of known techniques
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's core technical move is a genuinely new mathematical/algorithmic primitive (a new operation, kernel, objective, or construction not reducible to combining existing named techniques), versus an explicit combination/amalgamation/application of already-named existing techniques to a new setting. A 10 = a clearly new primitive is introduced. A 0 = the abstract explicitly describes combining, ensembling, or amalgamating multiple existing named methods.
proposals.rationale: R50 ('Optimizer Amalgamation', card_pct=0.893, dense_pct=0.214) explicitly combines a 'pool of teacher optimizers into a single student optimizer' -- pure recombination -- and is scorecard-favored. By contrast R23 (card_pct=0.068) introduces a genuinely new coreset construction technique and R58 (card_pct=0.047) introduces a new functional ELBO defined directly on stochastic processes -- both are new primitives that the scorecard scores near zero.

proposals.name: Grandiose opening framing vs narrow delivered contribution
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the GAP between how sweeping/important the abstract's opening sentence claims the problem area to be, and how narrow/specific the actual technical contribution delivered later in the abstract turns out to be. A 10 = a sweeping opening claim ('one of the primary open questions in AI', 'bridging two fields') followed by a narrow, specific technical fix. A 0 = the opening framing is modest and proportionate to the actual scope of the contribution delivered.
proposals.rationale: R47 (card_pct=0.966) opens by declaring HPO 'one of the primary open questions in AI' before delivering a specific rank-based surrogate model; R16 (card_pct=0.761) opens by claiming to 'bridge the two fields of finite-agent and infinite-agent games' before delivering a policy-conditioning hypernetwork. Both large opening claims relative to narrow deliveries are scorecard-favored (dense_pct 0.385 and 0.291 respectively), while R40 (dense_pct=0.996) opens with no grandiose framing at all, matching its narrow, direct technical scope.

proposals.name: Exhaustive success-and-failure accounting vs single top-line number
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract reports a COMPLETE accounting of outcomes -- both where the method succeeds and where/how often it fails, or a full bidirectional pattern -- rather than only a single best-case aggregate or highlight number. A 10 = the abstract states both a success rate/condition AND the complementary failure/residual case explicitly (the two parts account for the full space of outcomes). A 0 = only a single top-line aggregate or highlight number is given, with no acknowledgment of the complementary failure cases.
proposals.rationale: R33 (dense_pct=0.987) states it finds 'an adversarial example for 4.38% of samples, and a certificate of robustness ... for the remainder' -- a complete, exhaustive partition. R09 (dense_pct=0.618) reports a bidirectional failure: classifiers trained on original data fail on revised data 'and vice versa'. Both dense-favored. By contrast R05/IRIS (card_pct=0.932) reports only the highlight number 'outperforms humans on 10 out of 26 games' with no mention of the other 16 games or any failure accounting.

proposals.name: New reusable dataset or benchmark contributed alongside method
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly states that the paper contributes a NEW reusable dataset, benchmark, or testbed to the community (not just a method evaluated on existing data). A 10 = the abstract explicitly states a new dataset/benchmark is created and released. A 0 = the paper evaluates purely on existing benchmarks/datasets with no new data/resource contribution mentioned.
proposals.rationale: R09 (dense_pct=0.618) states 'We will publicly release both datasets' as an explicit resource contribution, and R37 (dense_pct=0.731) generates and releases a new synthetic dataset (GINC) specifically to enable clean study of the phenomenon. Both are dense-favored. By contrast R47 (card_pct=0.966) evaluates on 86 pre-existing datasets with no new resource contributed, and R55 (card_pct=1.000) likewise contributes no new dataset -- both scorecard-favored despite offering nothing new to the community's data pool.

proposals.name: Numeric benchmark result density
proposals.instruction: Count how many distinct quantitative result figures (percentages, point deltas, ratios, parameter/FLOP counts, benchmark scores) the abstract states explicitly. Score 0 if none are mentioned, 10 if five or more distinct quantitative figures appear. Do not judge whether the reported numbers are impressive, correct, or well-supported -- score only how much explicit numeric quantification of results is present in the text.
proposals.rationale: R07 packs in '10.9% and 12.4% improvement in MAE' and R53 stacks six separate percentages ('40%', '0.5%', '2.8%', '43%', '0.8%', '3%'); this dense-numeral reporting style is a writing convention that a scorecard rubric can reward point-by-point regardless of whether the underlying claims constitute better research than a paper like R11 or R32 that reports no numbers at all.

proposals.name: Code/data release statement presence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how explicitly the abstract states that code, data, or trained models will be or are being released (e.g., a repository URL, 'code is available at...', 'we release our implementation'). 0 = no release statement of any kind; 10 = an explicit, specific release statement naming a repository. Do not judge whether releasing code says anything about the work's quality -- score only whether the statement is textually present.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R28 both end with an explicit GitHub link and release statement while similarly-scoped papers like R08 and R11 make no release claim at all; packaging and hosting a public repo takes engineering time that better-resourced groups have more of, so this can be predictive of scorecard favor without being a research-quality signal per se (though well-resourced groups may also do better work, hence mixed).

proposals.name: Formal proof/guarantee vocabulary density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract uses formal proof or guarantee language ('we prove', 'theorem', 'lemma', 'guarantee(s)', 'converge(s)/convergence', 'bound'). 0 = none of this vocabulary appears; 10 = the abstract is saturated with such terms. Do not judge whether any proofs are correct, tight, or important -- score only the presence of this vocabulary register.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('we prove that LookAhead converges locally to equilibria') and R44 ('We give theoretical proof that our method is stable and non-dissipative') both use this register heavily; this is a subfield dialect marker (theory vs. applied-empirical ML writing) that can shift a text-only reader's impression independent of whether the underlying contribution is strong.

proposals.name: Wordplay/rhetorical-device title
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the title uses a rhetorical device -- wordplay, pun, metaphor, or a deliberate riff on a familiar phrase or an existing well-known method's name -- rather than being a plain literal description of the method. 0 = fully literal/technical title; 10 = the title is built entirely around a rhetorical flourish. Do not judge whether the title is clever, memorable, or appropriate -- score only how much of this device is present.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('Fix your classifier'), R47 ('Chaos is a Ladder'), and R41 (riffing on the well-known 'You Only Look Once' phrasing) are all dense_high_card_low; a catchy title can leave an impression on a holistic reader that a checklist-based scorecard never scores, regardless of actual novelty.
proposals.upstream_parent: author marketing savvy / idiomatic writing fluency

proposals.name: Explicit enumerated contribution structure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the abstract's contributions are presented as an explicit enumerated/ordinal list ('First,... Second,...', 'i)/ii)/iii)', 'three-fold', numbered contribution markers). 0 = pure flowing prose with no enumeration; 10 = contributions are fully itemized with explicit ordinal markers throughout. Do not judge whether the enumeration makes the abstract clearer or better organized -- score only whether the device is present.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('First, we present... Second, we identify... Third, we present... Fourth, we evaluate...') and R35 ('three-fold... i) the population-size encoding... ii) a hypernetwork... iii) the population size') both use heavy ordinal scaffolding; a criterion-by-criterion scorecard judge can be primed to find and credit exactly this many discrete 'contributions' independent of their substance.

proposals.name: Named-lab/org self-branding in text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the abstract text (including any embedded URL) identifies a specific, recognizable research-group or consortium brand name (e.g., a lab name embedded in a code-repository organization path, or a named project associated with one identifiable group) rather than an anonymous individual username or no identity marker at all. 0 = no identifiable group brand anywhere in the text; 10 = a specific group/lab brand name appears explicitly and prominently. Do not judge whether that group's reputation is deserved -- score only whether a group identity is textually visible.
proposals.rationale: Both R06 and R36 embed the same 'VITA-Group' GitHub organization name in their code links, and both are dense_low_card_high with high card_pct (.637 and .893); a scorecard reading only text could be picking up on a recognizable brand signature that a dense holistic reader either weights differently or does not notice as a discrete 'criterion' at all.

proposals.name: Experimental-scale enumeration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how explicitly the abstract enumerates the SCALE of its experimental protocol -- specific counts of baselines, datasets, tasks, languages, or named compute hardware (e.g., 'X baselines', 'Y datasets', 'TPUv3 Pod', '44 languages'). 0 = no scale figures given anywhere; 10 = multiple explicit scale counts are stated. Do not judge whether that scale is sufficient, well-designed, or necessary -- score only how much explicit scale-quantification appears in the text.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces, 86 datasets/tasks') and R55 ('up to 44 languages in our experiment') both foreground large-N experimental scale; running that many configurations requires compute and engineering time that correlates with institutional resourcing, which can inflate scorecard 'thoroughness' criteria independent of whether the core idea is good (mixed because well-resourced labs may also genuinely validate better).

proposals.name: Trend/hype-keyword density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how many currently-fashionable subfield buzzwords appear in the abstract (e.g., 'GPT', 'in-context learning', 'diffusion', 'Transformer', 'large language model', 'foundation model'). 0 = no such terms appear; 10 = the abstract is dense with such terms throughout. Do not judge whether the use of these terms is warranted, accurate, or central to the contribution -- score only the raw presence of this vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: R27 foregrounds 'GPT-3', 'in-context learning', and 'large language models' repeatedly, and R51 foregrounds 'diffusion-based' throughout; papers submitted while a topic is peaking may draw disproportionate attention from both a dense reader's learned priors and a scorecard's topic-relevance criteria, independent of the paper's own contribution quality (mixed since genuinely important work also clusters on hot topics).

proposals.name: Named prior-algorithm/author citation density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the abstract explicitly names specific prior algorithms, methods, or authors inline (e.g., a named baseline algorithm like 'LARS', an inline citation like 'Author et al. (Year)', or a conference-tagged reference like 'SODA'12'). 0 = no named prior work anywhere in the text; 10 = multiple specific named methods or authors appear inline. Do not judge whether the citations are appropriate, complete, or accurately characterized -- score only how much explicit naming occurs.
proposals.rationale: R10 names 'LARS' as a specific prior algorithm to beat and R58 chains three inline dated citations ('Feldman and Schulman, SODA'12', 'Huang et al., FOCS'18', 'Braverman et al., FOCS'22'); positioning a paper explicitly within a named lineage can signal insider community standing to a text reader, which is a network/visibility effect distinct from the quality of the new contribution (mixed since genuine scholarly grounding also produces this pattern).

proposals.name: Niche/narrow application-domain framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the abstract frames its contribution around a narrow, specialized, non-mainstream-ML application domain or dataset (e.g., a specific biological species, an astrophysical imaging instrument, a single named game) rather than a general/mainstream ML benchmark or task class. 0 = framed entirely around mainstream general ML benchmarks/tasks; 10 = framed entirely around one narrow specialized application. Do not judge whether the narrow application is a good or interesting choice -- score only how narrow/specialized the framing is.
proposals.rationale: R23 frames its entire contribution around 'Zebrafish Swim Bout Classification' and R42 around 'astrophysical multispectral imaging'; both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting a scorecard rubric with domain-specific extent criteria (e.g., 'is the target application clearly specified and validated') is easy to satisfy fully within a narrow, self-contained niche, while a dense holistic reader may discount niche applied papers relative to more general contributions (mixed since a narrow domain can also be where the genuinely hardest, best work happens).

proposals.name: Concrete failure diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract identifies a specific failure mode, explains its technical cause, and distinguishes it from generic shortcomings; give 0 when motivation is only broad importance or a list of limitations.
proposals.rationale: R02 defines spuriousness through confounding and causal effects, while R58 pinpoints conditions causing unstable uncertainty estimates. These concrete diagnoses contrast with more generic motivation in R33 and R37.

proposals.name: Design-to-failure linkage
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when each main proposed component is explicitly tied to a diagnosed failure through a plausible mechanism; give 0 when components are an unexplained bundle or merely an architecture name.
proposals.rationale: R09 links boundary-focused regularization to degenerate sampling, and R24 links gradient regularization to quantization perturbations. R50 similarly ties discriminator redesign to semantic alignment, providing unusually clear design logic.

proposals.name: Theory-to-design translation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when formal analysis yields a concrete objective, parameterization, algorithm, or prediction used by the method; give 0 when theory is absent, ornamental, or disconnected from the method.
proposals.rationale: R07 converts process-level KL theory into finite measurement objectives, R12 turns mean-field depth scales into trainability implications, and R30 derives layers from an SDP condition.

proposals.name: Assumption discipline
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract states assumptions and boundary conditions precisely and distinguishes what holds in each regime; give 0 when claims sound universal while conditions remain unstated.
proposals.rationale: R32 separates one-dimensional, general strongly convex, and quadratic cases; R40 distinguishes linear from nonlinear VAEs; R49 explicitly handles distribution mismatch through a synthetic HMM setting.

proposals.name: Pathology-centered design
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when pathological cases are intrinsic to the formulation and addressed by a targeted mechanism; give 0 when difficult cases are merely mentioned or ignored.
proposals.rationale: R08 builds around outliers, R27 targets graph perturbations without classifier access, and R54 handles exact adversarial verification. R44 likewise incorporates outliers and non-rigid deformation into the formulation.

proposals.name: Structure-aware inductive bias
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the representation or operation encodes meaningful geometry, symmetry, topology, spectrum, or invariance of the data; give 0 when the inductive bias is generic and unrelated to data structure.
proposals.rationale: R06 uses spectral graph structure, R18 encodes spherical rotational equivariance, R51 incorporates topology, and R29 combines spectral low- and high-pass behavior.

proposals.name: Long-range information preservation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract gives an explicit route for accessing information across many layers, hops, scales, or time steps and explains why it remains stable; give 0 when dependencies are only asserted or handled by adding depth.
proposals.rationale: R05 constructs multi-scale graph information, R19 proves preservation of long-range graph information, and R55 adds graph reasoning for long-distance textual relationships.

proposals.name: Shift robustness
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the method explicitly handles changing dictionaries, populations, domains, demonstrations, or reward regimes through a named adaptation variable; give 0 when it assumes one fixed regime with no adaptation mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses counterfactual data, R10 handles variable mixing matrices, R17 models changing dynamics, and R48 targets rewards that generalize beyond demonstrated states.

proposals.name: Resource-quality co-optimization
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the method jointly addresses a resource bottleneck and a quality constraint with concrete computational, memory, or iteration implications; give 0 when efficiency is a vague afterthought or treated separately.
proposals.rationale: R04 connects large batches to sharply reduced training time, R18 reduces equivariant-layer complexity, R47 uses sampling for scalable graph training, and R20 removes a costly classifier layer.

proposals.name: Unifying abstraction
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when one formal framework explains multiple prior methods and yields a clearly identified extension or common principle; give 0 when “unified” means only combining modules or benchmarking variants.
proposals.rationale: R05 connects Lanczos networks to diffusion maps, R18 generalizes several spherical CNN approaches, and R30 places diverse Lipschitz architectures under one algebraic condition.

proposals.name: Multiplicity awareness
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the formulation explicitly represents multiple valid solutions, latent alternatives, uncertainty, or multimodality and explains how learning uses them; give 0 when it forces a single target despite stated ambiguity.
proposals.rationale: R23 makes solution multiplicity central to combinatorial learning, R50 models multimodal image synthesis, R58 addresses aleatoric uncertainty, and R49 models shared latent concepts.

proposals.name: Claim-aligned validation
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the validation setup directly varies the phenomenon the paper addresses and includes a relevant control or comparison; give 0 when evaluation is only generic benchmarking unrelated to the proposed mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R24 varies quantization bit-width, R43 tests progressive-reward and ordinary-reward settings, and R54 evaluates exact bounded perturbation robustness. Each evaluation mirrors the paper’s central technical claim.

proposals.name: Contribution attribution
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract describes ablations or controlled contrasts that isolate individual components, losses, or design choices; give 0 when no component-level contrast is described and attribution is impossible from the text.
proposals.rationale: R58 identifies the likelihood loss as the culprit before introducing β-NLL, while R38 traces predictions to experimental artifacts and tests their removal. Both support component-level causal attribution.

proposals.name: Explanatory insight
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract explains a surprising phenomenon with a mechanism that yields a non-obvious, testable implication; give 0 when it offers only a method description without explaining behavior.
proposals.rationale: R12 explains trainability through chaos and signal propagation, R25 explains adversarial vulnerability through linearity, and R49 explains in-context learning through latent document concepts.

proposals.name: Problem reframing
proposals.instruction: Give 10 when the paper makes a previously neglected variable or objective central and derives formal consequences for learning; give 0 when it is a routine architectural or tuning modification with no new problem perspective.
proposals.rationale: R23 reframes combinatorial learning around multiple valid solutions, R59 jointly learns the clustering algorithm and distance metric, and R49 reframes in-context learning as latent-concept inference.

proposals.name: Abstract length
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 (very brief) to 10 (very long) how much text, sentence count, and elaboration the abstract contains; judge extent only, not whether the additional detail is good or useful.
proposals.rationale: Length is a visible verbosity proxy that can influence processing independently of research quality. R08 and R44 are highly elaborated, whereas R32 is only a title.

proposals.name: Novelty rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract uses explicit novelty, priority, surprise, or state-of-the-art language; judge only the presence of such wording, not whether the claims are justified or important.
proposals.rationale: Promotional novelty vocabulary can act as a stylistic cue without establishing research quality. R02, R06, and R53 repeatedly use terms such as novel, new, or surprising.

proposals.name: Method-acronym branding
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract introduces branded method names, capitalized acronyms, or multiple named components; judge naming density only, not whether the names improve the work.
proposals.rationale: Professional presentation or marketing assistance may leave a distinctive naming fingerprint that attracts attention without changing the underlying work. R01, R10, and R33 use prominent bespoke method labels and acronyms.

proposals.name: Canonical benchmark cues
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract mentions recognizable canonical datasets, architectures, tasks, or hardware associated with established ML communities; judge familiarity cues only, not the importance or quality of those resources.
proposals.rationale: Receiving-side familiarity can make certain textual references salient independently of research quality. R17 names MNIST and ReLU networks, while R28 names BERT, ResNet-50, ImageNet, and TPU hardware.

proposals.name: Numerical-result density
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract contains exact percentages, metric values, speedups, dataset counts, complexity orders, or other numerical performance details; judge quantity of numbers only, not whether the results are favorable or credible.
proposals.rationale: Well-resourced teams may generate more measured comparisons, leaving a numerical fingerprint; those resources can also contribute to genuine research quality. R17 and R28 contain many precise computational and performance figures.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract claims coverage across multiple datasets, languages, domains, tasks, architectures, or transfer settings; judge breadth of described coverage only, not whether it is adequate or convincing.
proposals.rationale: Large teams and greater infrastructure can support broad evaluations, while also potentially improving genuine research quality. R04 spans up to 44 languages, and R11 reports 86 datasets across 16 search spaces.

proposals.name: Formalism density
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract contains theorem, proof, bound, assumption, equation, or mathematically formal terminology; judge formalism extent only, not rigor, correctness, or research value.
proposals.rationale: Theoretical training and community norms leave visible formal-language fingerprints, and may also affect genuine quality. R08 and R24 foreground bounds, phases, and influence-function analysis, while R44 emphasizes formal coreset guarantees.

proposals.name: Editorial polish
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the prose is grammatically smooth, standardized, cohesive, and free of apparent typographical or terminology inconsistencies; judge surface polish only, not whether the writing makes the research better.
proposals.rationale: Professional editing can improve textual presentation without changing research quality. R03 and R20 use highly standardized exposition, while R22 contains noticeably denser and less polished phrasing.

proposals.name: Trend vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract uses currently fashionable model, problem, or framing terms in machine learning; judge presence of zeitgeist vocabulary only, not whether the topic is important or technically strong.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing and field trends can influence terminology independently of research quality. R02 foregrounds diffusion models, R34 foregrounds Transformers and world models, and R45 foregrounds GPT-3 and in-context learning.

proposals.name: Artifact-availability cues
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract advertises code, pretrained models, datasets, repositories, or reproducibility artifacts; judge the presence of availability statements only, not whether the artifacts are useful or the research is sound.
proposals.rationale: Well-supported groups and open-source-oriented communities leave artifact-sharing fingerprints, while those resources can also facilitate genuine quality. R07, R10, and R19 explicitly mention publicly available code or models.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Explanatory Depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a causal account of why the method addresses the stated failure and derives testable implications; score 0 when it merely introduces components and asserts usefulness.
proposals.rationale: R06, R20, and R60 explicitly connect architectural behavior to signal propagation, latent concepts, or adversarial vulnerability, unlike abstracts with primarily procedural descriptions.

proposals.name: Theory-Practice Coupling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the analysis directly constrains, explains, or predicts the behavior of the proposed method; score 0 when theory is detached from the method or offers only generic guarantees.
proposals.rationale: R21 and R44 tie convergence or stability claims directly to their architectures, while R45 connects finite-width analysis to observable interpolation behavior.

proposals.name: Bottleneck-to-Complexity Fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a concrete computational bottleneck is identified and the method changes complexity or resource use in a directly matched way; score 0 when efficiency is asserted without a specific bottleneck-to-design connection.
proposals.rationale: R08, R18, and R23 explicitly match sampling or architectural changes to graph, spherical, or large-batch computational constraints.

proposals.name: Failure-Mode Diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract isolates a specific failure mechanism, states conditions that produce it, and gives a targeted remedy; score 0 when it gives only a broad problem statement and an undifferentiated modification.
proposals.rationale: R14 analyzes manifold-support behavior, R27 identifies pathological variance-learning conditions, and R37 discovers artifact-driven predictions before proposing correction.

proposals.name: Threat-Model Completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when robustness claims specify the perturbation, adversary, or distribution shift and explain why the method addresses that threat; score 0 when robustness is claimed without defining the threat conditions.
proposals.rationale: R09, R25, and R38 make perturbation mechanisms and attacker or verifier assumptions explicit, providing unusually concrete robustness framing.

proposals.name: Structural Inductive-Bias Fit
